definition: Building a business career by buying and stewarding an existing company.
The linked work of finding, agreeing, investigating, funding and completing a business purchase.
An estimate of sustainable operating earnings after explicitly justified adjustments to reported EBITDA.
The scheduled repayment of a loan’s principal over time.
Borrowing sized in part against the eligible lending value of identifiable assets.
Borrowing from a bank under agreed repayment, pricing, security and conduct terms.
Acquisitions added to an existing company or group rather than built as a wholly separate platform.
Intermediaries who help sellers, buyers or borrowers find and progress suitable counterparties.
The buyer or sponsor’s ownership interest and any cash capital they contribute to the acquisition.
The combination of debt, seller funding and equity used to finance a transaction.
The timing and amount of money entering and leaving a business.
Assets or rights pledged to support a lender’s recovery if obligations are not met.
Contractual promises and tests that constrain a borrower’s finances or actions.
Dependence on a small number of customers or a shared source of demand.
The interest, fees and other financial costs attached to a borrowing arrangement.
Cash required to meet debt interest and principal payments during a period.
An agreed part of the purchase price scheduled for payment after completion.
Investigation that tests the purchase assumptions and identifies risks before a binding commitment.
Purchase payments whose entitlement or amount depends on agreed future performance conditions.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization; an operating comparison measure rather than spendable cash.
The negotiated value of the operating business before the agreed bridge to shareholder proceeds.
The value attributable to shareholders after the agreed adjustments from enterprise value.
Lending associated with a public support or guarantee scheme whose terms depend on its specific program.
Borrowing provided through an institutional capital organization rather than informal personal funding.
Capital supplied for an ownership claim rather than a scheduled loan repayment.
MOIC compares value returned with money invested; IRR expresses a return rate using the timing of cash flows.
The use of borrowing to fund ownership, often measured as debt divided by annual earnings.
A preliminary record of the proposed purchase economics and the conditions for progressing a deal.
The people, responsibilities and reporting systems that keep the acquired business operating and accountable.
A person’s contractual promise to meet specified obligations if the primary borrower does not.
Equity with negotiated economic priority over another share class, such as priority in exit proceeds.
Credit supplied outside deposit-taking banking, often using capital committed by investors to a lending strategy.
Financing supported by eligible amounts customers owe for sales already made.
Replacing or revising existing borrowing with a new financing arrangement.
How shareholders realize value through distributions, sales or other liquidity events.
Building a group through repeated acquisitions of businesses intended to fit a common strategy.
An ownership interest the seller retains or receives as part of the consideration for a sale.
Purchase consideration the seller leaves at risk after completion through an agreed later-payment structure.
Debt granted priority over specified other claims under the financing arrangements.
Creating and qualifying a pipeline of businesses whose owners may consider a sale.
An agreement that places one creditor’s rights behind another’s in specified circumstances.
Choosing businesses whose economics, financing needs and operating demands fit the buyer.
A price expressed as a multiple of a clearly defined measure of annual earnings.
Money tied up in the everyday cycle of customers, stock, suppliers and other operating balances.
